title: I Need Time!
summary: Use the tempo gained by a rook sacrifice to promote with check before the opposing pawn can move.

nodes.question: What did the rook sacrifice buy?
nodes.explanation: After ...Rxg1, the black rook blocks its own g2 pawn. White has Kf6, f4 and g6 against Ke8, Rg1, f5 and g2. The g-pawn must move immediately.

branches.title: Use the tempo before the rook clears g1
commentary: Begin in the seven-piece phase after ...Rxg1 at 70 seconds. The preceding eight-piece Rg1 sacrifice remains source context, outside this exact checked tree.
g7 uses the tempo while Black’s own rook blocks g2 from promoting.
Rh1 clears the pawn’s promotion square, but costs Black a move.
g8=Q+ promotes with check, so Black cannot answer immediately with ...g1=Q.
Kd7 is the illustrated king retreat from the promotion check.
Qxg2 removes the dangerous passer. White retains an exactly checked queen-and-pawns versus rook-and-pawn win.

branches.title: The rook clears g1 on the other side
commentary: This independent representative rook retreat tests the same timing idea on the other side of g1.
g7 takes the essential promotion tempo.
Rf1 clears g1, but f4 blocks the rook’s line toward Kf6, so this move does not give check.
g8=Q+ promotes with check before the black pawn can advance.
Kd7 is an independently selected legal reply, matching the source’s king retreat in the other rook line.
Qxg2 removes the passer and retains the exact White win; further rook conversion is not invented.

exercises.prompt: Why is a rook allowed to capture White’s rook?
exercises.answer: After the source’s ...Rxg1, the capturing rook occupies its own pawn’s promotion square. That obstruction gives White the time needed to push g7.

exercises.prompt: Why does promotion with check matter?
exercises.answer: The check forces Black to answer with the king before playing ...g1=Q. White can then use Qxg2 to eliminate the pawn.
